source: Del et al. (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models
finding: Three open reasoning models, 17 tasks. Verbalized confidence (VC) from a run beats self-consistency (SC) at equal sample counts. SC does not overtake VC up to K=8. VC averaged over samples giving the majority answer gains most in maths.
numbers: AUROC, VC: maths K=1 71.3 to K=8 81.4 (+10.1); STEM +4.6, humanities +4.1, front-loaded and mostly flat after K=5. SC at K=2: maths 70.5, STEM 66.6, humanities 63.3, each below VC. MMLU-Pro Math: SC@2 65.9 vs VC@1 78.8; GSM8K 63.3 vs 68.7. Models gpt-oss-20b (high effort), Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-8B; up to 60K tokens per sample.
quote: SC starts substantially below VC across all domains
limits: Open mid-sized models only, not frontier closed ones. Numeric VC elicited with the Tian EpEL prompt. Bootstrap from up to 100 samples per question. Tasks mostly multiple choice. This reverses the 2023 Xiong result (consistency beat verbalized) for reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 answered for reasoning models: do not replace a stated confidence with agreement among 2-3 samples. Keep both. Stated confidence from a reasoning model is already usable; extra samples add most up to K about 5.

source: Del et al. (2026) - hybrid estimator, domains and matched tokens
finding: Combining agreement with verbalized confidence beats scaling either alone. With K=2 the hybrid already beats VC or SC at K=8. Gain flattens early outside maths.
numbers: Hybrid (SCVC) at K=2 vs single-run VC: +12.9 AUROC in maths, +6.4 in STEM and humanities. Maths hybrid adds +2.7 from K=2 to 5 and +1.5 from K=5 to 8. STEM and humanities about +1 to 2 beyond K=2. Matched-token check on GPT-OSS-20B: SC is markedly weaker under extended reasoning than under short generation, across maths, physics, psychology.
quote: the hybrid estimator improves AUROC by up to +12 on average
limits: Equal-weight sum (alpha 0.5), robust to weights per paper. Gain depends on domain: biggest in maths, where these models got RL on verifiable rewards. Each sample is a full chain of thought, so K=2 costs two traces. Not tested on agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the knee is at N=2 for a hybrid and at about N=5 for averaged stated confidence. N=9 buys little outside maths. Our schema can set N=3 and combine agreement with the stated number.

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Self-consistency and cross-model agreement as confidence signals
finding: 265,000 samples from 53 runners on GPQA Diamond and AIME (K=50 per case). Agreement among samples is a positive but weak predictor of majority-correctness. It is worst for the most consistent model.
numbers: Spearman rho of agreement with majority-correctness 0.20 to 0.59, all 12 cell tests positive after Holm correction. gpt-4.1 on GPQA: agreement 0.89, rho 0.19, no accuracy gain over gpt-4.1-mini (agreement 0.82, rho 0.42). Agreement 0.8 or more on 77% of GPQA entries, and 48% of those were wrong.
quote: agreement is a positive but weak predictor
limits: GPT-4.1 family and small variants, not reasoning models; exploratory Claude check (haiku-4.5, sonnet-4.6, opus-4.7) only. Not preregistered. 394 unique cases, 5,300 rows, runners wrote their own prompts.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 answered in part: yes, sample agreement is often confidently wrong, and it gets worse as the model gets more consistent. Treat agreement as a conditional signal; add an outside check.

source: Ding (2026) - recurring confident errors and signal comparison
finding: Confident wrong answers recur across runners, prompts and model families, so they are not sampling noise. No single confidence signal dominated on 50 cases.
numbers: gpt-4.1 on GPQA: 28% of unique cases confidently wrong (agreement >=0.8, sample accuracy <=0.3) for every runner; 50% for at least one. gpt-4.1-mini, GPQA n=50: Spearman with correctness agreement 0.31 [0.05, 0.57], verbalized 0.21 [-0.10, 0.49], P(True) 0.19 [-0.10, 0.45]; AURC verbalized 0.30 vs agreement 0.44; rank-average combo ECE 0.13 vs agreement 0.30.
limits: n=50 per benchmark; verbalized parsed on only 39 of 50 GPQA cases, so its AURC is on a favourable subset. AIME errors are dispersed, not shared. Some GPQA items may be mislabelled.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: a combination of agreement and stated confidence was best calibrated, matching d02. Shared errors set a floor on what any same-model vote can fix.

source: Denisov-Blanch et al. (2026) Consensus is Not Verification: why crowd-wisdom strategies fail for LLM truthfulness
finding: On five benchmarks without a verifier, polling many samples gives no consistent accuracy gain over one sample, even at 25x cost. LLM errors are strongly correlated within and across model families, so confidence-weighting and surprisingly-popular voting also fail.
numbers: 25 samples per model at temperature 0.7 and 1.0. MATH: plurality-wrong rate 3.9-25.8%, and the most common wrong answer makes up 65-87% of wrong responses. AIME: plurality-wrong 3.9-75.8%, concentration 20-63%. HLE subset: accuracy 5.7%, far below the 50% guessing level. Random-string control: models still agree above chance.
quote: aggregation fails to provide a robust truth signal because language model errors are strongly correlated
limits: Open-source models; forecasting questions after the cutoff were all at chance. Authors say this does not contradict self-consistency in verified domains such as maths and code.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: where no checker exists, N samples from one model mostly repeat the same error. Use samples where code, tests or a lookup can verify.

source: Upravitelev et al. (2026) Multiperspectivity as a resource for narrative similarity prediction (31-persona ensemble)
finding: 31 LLM personas on SemEval-2026 Task 4. Majority vote beats any single persona. Personas with concrete analytic frameworks are weaker alone but their errors are less correlated.
numbers: Ensemble test accuracy 0.705 (13th of 47 teams). Cross-model majority vote on dev 0.7025. Table 5 (garbled in extraction, so medium confidence): error correlation about 0.39 for practitioner personas against about 0.46 for lay personas; the text says errors are 19% less correlated for practitioners. Lay personas take the top 5 individual ranks.
limits: Not a calibration study; a narrative-similarity task with a hard-to-define gold label. Three open models. Gains came with weakened independence, not removed correlation.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: varying persona across samples lowers error correlation a little but does not remove it. Cheap to try, small effect. Not tested for confidence AUROC.

source: Kaddour et al. (2026) Agentic Uncertainty Reveals Agentic Overconfidence - pre vs post execution
finding: 100 SWE-bench Pro tasks, three frontier models (GPT-5.2-Codex, Gemini-3-Pro, Claude Opus 4.5). All were overconfident before, during and after. Reading the finished patch did not beat judging the task beforehand.
numbers: True success rates 35%, 22%, 27%. Post-execution estimates 73% (GPT), 77% (Gemini). AUROC pre vs post: GPT 0.62 vs 0.58, Claude 0.64 vs 0.55, Gemini 0.53 vs 0.51. Bootstrap CIs wide, for example GPT pre 0.62 [0.50, 0.75], post 0.58 [0.46, 0.70]; no pair significant alone. Mid-run checks at 25/50/75%: GPT AUROC stable at 0.53, Gemini 0.49 to 0.64, Claude 0.62 to 0.52. Doubt rose equally for successes and failures.
quote: pre-execution assessment with strictly less information tends to yield better discrimination
limits: The post-execution agent reviews the patch with read tools; it did not run the tests, so this is reflection, not test results. Same model solves and judges. 100 tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 answered in part: reflection alone did not improve discrimination and kept overconfidence high. Any gain must come from running tests, not from asking the model again. A test-result arm is still needed.

source: Kaddour et al. (2026) - adversarial 'find bugs' framing
finding: Asking the reviewer to hunt for bugs before giving a probability cut overconfidence and gave the best calibration. This is an LLM test of a counter-case step, close to Koriat 1980.
numbers: Overconfidence drops by up to 15 points. Overconfident-failure rate 72% to 45%. Table 2 ECE standard post to adversarial: Gemini 0.66 to 0.53; Claude 0.37 to 0.24; GPT 0.42 to 0.30. AUROC adversarial: Claude 0.64, Gemini 0.57, GPT 0.55 (no gain for GPT; pre-execution 0.62). Overconfidence still +0.20 to +0.40 after the adversarial step.
limits: No arm with a balanced pro-and-con step and no equal-token control, so Gap 4 is not closed. Coding review only. Estimates are still far from calibrated.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 in part: a counter-case step lowered ECE for 3 of 3 models and kept or raised AUROC for 2 of 3. Cheap to add at the end of an attempt. The pro/con and no-step arms are still missing.

source: Kaddour et al. (2026) - false consensus across models and ensembling
finding: Three different frontier models agree on the predicted outcome but are mostly wrong when they agree. Adversarial framing breaks this false consensus.
numbers: Standard pre-execution: all three models agree on pass/fail for 87% of tasks, only 13% of those agreements correct. Adversarial: three-way agreement 44%, 38% of agreements correct. Ensembles of pre and post: average cut GPT ECE from 0.42 to 0.32; the max rule gave the best GPT AUROC 0.68 but worst overconfidence.
limits: Binary outcome at a 50% threshold; base rates 22-35% so 'predict pass' is mostly wrong. Cross-model, not same-model samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: agreement among different models can also be wrongly confident when all share the same optimistic prior. Reframing the question changed agreement more than adding samples would.

source: Barkan, Black, Sourbut (2025) Do Large Language Models Know What They Are Capable Of?
finding: LLMs are overconfident in advance; graded outcomes in context change behaviour more than discrimination. Contract experiment: 9 sequential coding contracts, +1 dollar on success, -1 on failure, each with a 50% chance of being solvable.
numbers: 512 sequences of 9 contracts. AUROC rises only slightly or not at all (GPT 4.1 slight, Sonnet 3.5 none). All models' predicted success stays above 0.5 after earlier outcomes where half failed. Sonnet 3.5 cuts acceptance to about 50% with a small drop in stated confidence (risk aversion), and profit rises. GPT 4.1 stays near zero profit. Decisions fit expected-utility given their own stated probabilities.
quote: some but not all LLMs reduce their overconfidence
limits: Same task class (BigCodeBench) throughout; no transfer test to a new class. No count of how many outcomes are enough (only up to 8 prior).
agent_relevance: Gap 6 in part: 8 outcomes in context do not make stated confidence usable. Gains come from acting cautiously, not from better ranking. Recalibrate in code from logs instead of hoping in-context learning does it.

source: Barkan et al. (2025) - confidence during multi-step tasks (SWE-bench Verified)
finding: Confidence asked after each tool call, 70-call budget, 10 models (5 OpenAI, 5 Claude). Progress did not usually help. Reflecting on the final answer helped some models.
numbers: All Claude Sonnet models became more overconfident as they progressed; only GPT 4o clearly less so. After-the-fact AUROC beat step-1 AUROC significantly for only 4 of 10 models (GPT 4o, 4.1, 5.1 none, o1). Sonnet AUROC rose early, then fell below its start, because confidence rose fast on eventual successes and slowly on eventual failures. Several Sonnet models improved AUROC when asked to reflect on the submitted answer.
limits: Test running is not isolated from other tool use. Reasoning models did as well or worse than non-reasoning ones.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: more steps do not raise reliability by themselves; an end-of-attempt reflection step helped some models. Do not trust mid-run confidence.

source: Michael, BenShushan, Bien, Moore (2026) Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
finding: Preregistered study, 11 LLMs, six question sets. Models are overconfident on average, with a human-like hard-easy effect: overconfident on hard tests, underconfident on easy ones.
numbers: Across question sets models report 88% confidence on average and are correct on 79%, about 9 points overconfident. Chat models on LifeEval: score 52.8%, ECE 0.150, mean confidence 66.5%, hard-easy coefficient 0.732 (Llama-3.1-8B 0.941). Question sets: SciQ 1000, LSAT-AR 230, SAT-EN 206, HaluEval-QA 2000, BoolQ, LifeEval 808. Some easy sets show accuracy 97% with confidence 92%, which is underconfidence.
quote: overconfidence is greatest on difficult tests; by contrast, easy tests actually show substantial underconfidence
limits: Question sets are existing benchmarks plus a made-up difficulty test (age at death), not random draws from a real task mix. Authors give a regression-to-the-mean reading and do not test representative sampling. No open-ended or agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. The size of the gap depends on how hard the set is, so one average number says little. Expect underconfidence on easy items; recalibration needs difficulty bands.

source: Michael et al. (2026) - hard-easy explanation and what it implies
finding: Authors explain the hard-easy effect as regression to the mean: confidence responds less than accuracy when difficulty changes (citing Erev et al. 1994, Krueger and Mueller 2002).
numbers: No new test of representative sampling. Chat-model accuracy by set spans about 59% to 99% in Table 7, so the overconfidence mean mixes very different regimes.
limits: Same limits as d12. The Gigerenzer-Juslin dispute (hand-picked hard items) is untested because items were not drawn at random from a natural environment.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: this effect is expected from noisy confidence alone, so it is not proof of a human-like bias. Report overconfidence by difficulty band, not as one number.

source: Sicilia, Inan, Alikhani (2024) Accounting for Sycophancy in Language Model Uncertainty Estimation
finding: User suggestions that carry a stated confidence ('I am about z% sure I am correct') change both accuracy and the model's uncertainty. Hedging by the user helps larger models. Platt scaling with user-behaviour dummy variables (SyRoUP) repairs the Brier score.
numbers: 3,900 questions (conversation forecasting plus QA). With wrong user suggestions and null confidence, accuracy bias in forecasting: LLaMA3.1 8B 45.4 points, Mistral 7B 39.2, Mixtral 8x22B 38.5, Qwen2 72B 21.0. Hedging: Mixtral 38.5 to 35.3, Qwen2 21.0 to 17.4; small models do not respond. In QA all models show lower bias when users give low confidence. BSS of SyRoUP vs plain Platt at user-correctness 0/25/75/100%: 7.3/4.9/7.3/13.1 vs 6.5/4.7/2.6/2.0.
limits: 2024 open models (Llama 3.1, Mistral, Mixtral, Qwen2, Gemma2). The cue is a wrong suggested answer plus a certainty phrase, not a certainty phrase in the task statement. No frontier chat models. Stripping was not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 in part: user certainty does move accuracy toward the user. Whether stripping it at S1 recovers the loss is untested. Cheap test: same item with and without the certainty phrase.

source: Tao et al. (2025) Revisiting Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration of Large Language Models
finding: 80 LLMs on MMLU-Pro. Linguistic verbal uncertainty (hedge words like 'probably' scored by a judge model) beats numeric verbalized and token-probability signals. High accuracy does not imply good calibration (GPT-4.1 poorly calibrated).
numbers: About 10% better AUROC and ECE than the second-best method, averaged over 80 models. Kendall correlation between ECE and AUROC is near zero for the linguistic method (-0.071). Judge: Llama-4-Maverick scores the hedging in free text.
quote: LVU consistently outperforms both TPU and NVU methods
limits: This is not a test of a few fixed ordinal levels. The signal is free-text hedging scored by a judge, with no fixed scale and no sweep of the number of levels. Small models often skip hedges. One benchmark. Earlier note K27 should read hedge language, not 3-5 labelled levels.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open: no study sweeps the number of levels. Hedges carry signal, but an enforced small scale against 0-100 is untested.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for Confidence - sample sizes and design for a human baseline
finding: Exp 1: 73 paid volunteers, 68 kept, two-alternative general-knowledge items, 10 scored items per condition, control then a 'reasons for and against' condition. Exp 2: 200 volunteers, one reason for, against, or both after choosing; only the contradicting reason improved calibration.
numbers: Per item set 9-13 control and 10-12 reasons subjects. Fifteen items per set, first 5 dropped. Probability scale .5 to 1.0 in bins .5-.59 up to .9-.99 and 1.0. Exp 2: 11 subjects removed from the contradicting group for writing supporting reasons; a follow-up of 44 subjects tested the order. Control showed typical overconfidence; the reasons group kept overconfidence mostly at .9 and 1.0. The paper cites 'about 75% correct at .90' and 'p=1.00 wrong about 20%' from Fischhoff, Slovic, Lichtenstein (1977).
quote: The monotonic relationship between assessed probability and percentage correct indicates that people can monitor the correctness of their answers
limits: The PDF tables (Table 1 and 2 values, per-bin hit rates) were not readable in text extraction, so exact bin hit rates are NOT recorded. The 1977 paper was not opened. Jackknife tests over 68 reduced samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 only partly closed: design and N confirmed; per-bin table values still need reading from the page images. Do not quote per-bin hit rates from this note.

source: Jin et al. (2026) Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration
finding: The authors state that a temperature fitted on one domain does not generalize across domains, and run a cross-domain generative test (train PopQA, test TriviaQA). The test compares training-time methods, not a fitted temperature.
numbers: Table 3, Sem-ECE (lower is better), mean over 4 backbones: DPO/RLHF 0.0846, Reg 0.1015, CFT best-alpha 0.1109, label smoothing 0.6462 (collapse), their CALM 0.0671. Backbones Llama-3.1, Vicuna-7B, OLMo-2-7B, Mistral-7B.
limits: The temperature claim is asserted in the abstract, not measured. Open 7-8B models with token logits; verbalized confidence from a closed API is not covered. Sem-ECE is the authors' own metric.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no direct measurement of one-parameter recalibration on verbalized confidence across task classes. Li, Hale and Moore (2025) remain the best hint for per-class refits. Plan to refit per class from logged outcomes.
